McCarthy, Ph.D., is with Georgetown University, Washington, D. C. Intellectual debates over morality are one thing; policy formation is another. Sometimes there are clear correlations between law or policy and ethics, but that is the exception rather than the rule. Policy represents a response to pressure, interest, and public opinion as much as—if not more than—a deposit of community moral wisdom. Or is this dichotomy so clear? Perhaps a policy can be both politically pragmatic and morally wise. US policy and ethics concerning uses of animals in research illustrate the separation and complex connections among these levels of normative thought. This article will trace a selective and brief history of the movement to improve the treatment of animals involved in research, explain why that movement was largely ignored throughout most of the biomedical ethics revival of the last decades, and show the convergence of these currents in the development of US policy and regulations—although not in bioethics as a whole—over the past 25 yr. American animal rights and welfare movements have their origins in British antivivisection societies. Although animal experimentation had been conducted for centuries, it was not widespread until the nineteenth century. Before the discovery of anesthesia in 1846, all animal experimentation was conducted without any pain-relieving measures. Even after the advent of anesthesia, vivisection was often performed without palliatives of any kind, sometimes in flagrant violation of humane policy (Orlans 1993). The belief that animals did not feel pain (owing in part to the legacy of Cartesian dualism that viewed animals as automata) persisted through much of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. However, Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832) and later utilitarian philosophers—notably John Stuart Mill (1806–1873)—put the issue of pain at the center of their moral philosophy and proposed legal reforms for animal protection. Bentham and Mill believed that if animals could experience and anticipate pain, they deserved moral consideration regardless of any other apparent differences between humans and animals. Bentham summed up his argument in a passage cited repeatedly by animal advocates today: “The question is not, can they reason? nor, can they talk? but can they suffer?” (Bentham 1789). Long before organized opposition to cruelty to animals arose in England, the British had earned the reputation of being animal lovers—a “nation of pet-keepers,” as one London magazine quipped. (See Harriet Ritvo’s important discussion of the British tradition of pet-keeping [Ritvo 1987].) The widespread practice of pet-keeping moved the British public to regard the use of vivisection as problematic at best. British legal action to protect animals began with the passing in 1822 of the Act to Prevent Cruel and Improper Treatment of Cattle or “Martin’s Act,” after Richard Martin, who introduced the bill in the House of Commons. title: Fulcrum: Quantitative, Governed Granularity for Microservice Boundaries with the RVx Inde
abstract: Microservice migrations often produce the opposite of their promise: a distributed monolith that carries the cost of distribution without its benefits. The root cause is that service boundaries are chosen by qualitative heuristics that ignore a boundary's runtime cost, how often services actually change and execute together, and the cognitive capacity of the owning team.We introduce the RVx Index, a composite, bounded, context-calibrated score for whether a boundary adds value or merely adds distributed complexity. RVx fuses three signals usually analyzed in isolation: Kinetic Efficiency (useful computation over total transaction time, from traces), Semantic Distinctness (functional independence from version-history temporal coupling), and Cognitive Load (static complexity normalized by team capacity). We prove structural properties (boundedness, monotonicity, soft weakest-link behavior, exponent identifiability) and calibrate thresholds per domain profile. The governing principle is Khan's Law: a boundary is only as valuable as its weakest dimension.We present Fulcrum, a sense-decide-actuate-verify governance loop under a safety gate; a Saga Complexity Score for transaction topology; and KM3, a portfolio maturity model. Treating the metric as a gaming target, we give a threat model, adversarial analysis (G1-G14), and conformance requirements (N1-N23). We specify a reproducible protocol and report controlled simulation plus construct validation on a real deployed AWS benchmark.This is a framework and controlled-validation paper, not an organic-production study; predictive claims are stated as falsifiable hypotheses. A labeled extension (RVx-A) applies the same form to agent tool boundaries under the Model Context Protocol. Comments: 98 pages, 10 figures. Methods and framework paper: formal properties, controlled simulation, and construct validation on a deployed AWS benchmark; production study specified as future work. title: Information and knowledge sharing about fertility preservation: Trans and non-binary people’s accounts
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The right to build a family is central to decision-making around reproductive health, social inclusion and citizenship. Yet, in societies that privilege cis-heteronormative ways of reproducing, individuals whose bodies, identities, and relationships exist outside of these norms may be susceptible to reproductive injustice during their fertility journeys. This is arguably the case for transgender and non-binary (trans) people involved in decision-making about their reproductive futures. METHODS: This article investigates barriers to the fertility preservation journeys of trans individuals making decisions about gamete freezing for gender transition-related reasons. The discussion draws primarily on data collected from an interview study with 13 trans people in Aotearoa New Zealand, aged between 19 and 30 years. Analyses of YouTube video blog and survey data support the discussion. FINDINGS: Study findings indicate a need for more information in a range of healthcare and educative settings about reproductive options for trans people; the presence of a generational shift in reproductive orientations for some participants toward the option of biogenetic parenthood as well as non-consanguineous forms of doing family; and relational decisionmaking about gamete freezing that is interactively negotiated with family and discussed with others, rather than purely agentic. CONCLUSION: To address the study findings, we call for healthcare professionals and social work practitioners to actively include the voices of trans and queer (LGBTQIA+) youth in education programming, policy, and decision-making as a step towards reimagining and securing equitable access to sexual and reproductive health, fertility care, and diverse reproductive paths for all people.

title: AskChem: Claim-Centered Infrastructure for Chemistry Literature Synthesis
abstract: Chemistry literature synthesis often requiresassembling specific findings scattered across many publications, yet existing literaturesearch systems primarily return ranked document lists.As a result, scientists and AI agents need to locate relevant information, trace each finding to its source, and assemble cross-paper answers manually.We present AskChem, a claim-centered infrastructure that changes the retrieval unit for cross-paper chemistry search from the paper to the source-linked claim.Available source text is converted into atomic, typed claims, each carrying a source DOI and a verbatim quote or an explicit evidence locator.Over this shared claim store, AskChem exposes complementary operational structures for search and synthesis: a corpus-induced faceted taxonomy stabilized for hierarchical retrieval and browsing, an automatically extracted evidence graph linking claims through typed relations, and an exploratory living taxonomy that situates indexed papers under scientific principles.At the frozen index snapshot, AskChem contains 2.4M claims from 147K papers, 30% processed from full text and 70% from abstracts only.The system provides a web interface, as well as REST, SDK, and MCP access for AI agents.On a 30-question AskChem-Bench pilot focused on citation traceability and paper relevance rather than factual-answer accuracy, grounding a GPT-5.5 reader in AskChem yields 100% resolvable DOIs, compared with 88.3% without retrieval, and the highest citation density among five tested systems.
